strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: associating global SD maps with online-constructed local HD maps to enable lane-level hybrid navigation, filling a clear gap left by prior online HD-map-construction literature.

Introduces a new, reasonably large-scale benchmark (OMA/OMA-GT) built from nuScenes + OpenStreetMap with over 30k scenes, 480k roads and 260k lane paths, along with a companion GT-based variant to isolate perception noise from association difficulty.

Proposes a tailored evaluation metric (Association P-R) that improves on prior Reachability P-R by adding label-sequence alignment and length-aware overlap checks, better reflecting navigation-relevant path correctness rather than pure point-wise distance.

The proposed Map Association Transformer (MAT) combines path-aware attention (topological, path-ordered) and spatial attention (space-filling-curve serialized, PTv3-inspired) with dual-axis RoPE, which is a sensible and reasonably well-motivated architectural design for this dual-graph matching problem.

Reasonably thorough ablations (attention components, RoPE, boundary input, loss combination, pooling strategy, patch size, grouping method) and a model family (MAT-T/S/M/L) demonstrating accuracy-latency trade-offs.
Provides qualitative analyses (attention-map visualizations, success/failure case studies) that offer some interpretability of what PA vs SA are learning.
weaknesses: Baselines are weak and dated: only classical KNN and HMM map-matching methods are compared against; no learning-based or graph-neural-network association baselines are evaluated, making it hard to assess how much of MAT's improvement stems from genuine architectural insight versus simply being a modern deep model against 1960s/2009-era heuristics.

Potential circularity/reproducibility concern in dataset construction: the automated labeling pipeline used to generate initial OMA annotations is itself a MAT model "trained on proprietary Chinese HD-SD maps" that is not described, released, or analyzed for label-quality bias — this could contaminate the benchmark and unfairly favor the proposed architecture, and it is not reproducible by other researchers.

Absolute performance remains low (best A-F1 ~42% on OMA, ~79% A-P on the easier OMA-GT setting), and the paper does not sufficiently discuss what this implies about real-world readiness or whether the task/metric design might be partly responsible.

Limited geographic/scenario diversity: data is sourced from only two nuScenes cities (Boston, Singapore), raising concerns about generalization to other road topologies and countries; the supplementary material's own domain-shift analysis (e.g., train vs. val road density, lane/road connectivity differences) suggests non-trivial train/test distribution mismatch that is not adequately addressed by the main paper's method or evaluation.

Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: path-aware attention is explicitly adapted from MapTRv2, spatial attention from Point Transformer v3, and RoPE from RoFormer; the core contribution is largely a combination/adaptation of existing components rather than fundamentally new mechanisms.
No variance/multiple-run reporting, statistical significance testing, or confidence intervals for the reported metrics, limiting confidence in the magnitude of reported gains over baselines.

Some presentation/clarity issues: several grammatical errors, and metric formulas (e.g., A-P50:95 defined as a raw sum over thresholds rather than a mean) appear inconsistent with the mAP convention referenced by the paper, which is confusing without clarification.

The supplementary material's re-training of MapTRv2 under a leakage-safe split reportedly caused a 'significant drop' in centerline quality that the authors say 'adversely affects OMA's current metrics,' yet the main paper does not transparently discuss this limitation or its implications for the validity of the reported OMA numbers.

strengths: The paper targets an under-explored and practically important problem: associating global SD-map roads with locally-constructed online HD-map centerlines to enable actual hybrid navigation, which is a meaningful gap relative to the large body of work purely on online HD map construction.

The dataset construction pipeline (nuScenes + OpenStreetMap, automated labeling followed by manual refinement) and the proposed Association P-R metric (with label-sequence alignment and length-aware overlap checks across multiple thresholds and length bins) represent a reasonable attempt to formalize evaluation for this new task.

The proposed MAT architecture combining path-aware attention (for topological/sequential structure) and spatial attention (via space-filling curve serialization) is a sensible design, and the ablation studies (Tables 3-5) reasonably isolate contributions of PA, SA, RoPE, boundary input, loss terms, and pooling strategy.

Reasonably thorough supplementary material, including attention-map visualizations, qualitative comparisons, failure-case analysis, and a family of model sizes (MAT-T/S/M/L) showing accuracy-latency trade-offs.
weaknesses: The only baselines compared against are classical, non-learning methods (KNN and HMM); there is no comparison to any other learned/graph-based/GNN association or map-matching method, or even a simplified transformer without the proposed dual-attention design, making it hard to attribute gains specifically to the proposed path-aware/spatial attention mechanisms versus simply using a learned model at all.

The dataset annotation process is circular/self-reinforcing: the OMA dataset's automated initial labels are produced by a MAT model pretrained on proprietary Chinese HD-SD maps, and this same architecture (MAT) is then evaluated as the proposed method on the resulting benchmark, raising concerns about benchmark validity and potential bias favoring the proposed architecture.

The authors themselves acknowledge in the supplementary material that using the proper ("pon") split with a retrained MapTRv2 for online HD map generation caused a "significant drop in the quality of the centerline network prediction," which they say "adversely affects OMA's current metrics," yet the main paper's results and conclusions do not reflect or resolve this issue, casting doubt on the reliability/reproducibility of the reported OMA numbers.

No end-to-end evaluation connecting map-association performance to actual downstream navigation or planning quality is provided, despite the paper's central motivation being enabling real hybrid navigation; the benefit of improved A-P/A-R/A-F1 for real driving performance is not demonstrated.

The dataset scale and diversity are limited (only Boston and Singapore, derived solely from nuScenes), which is modest relative to other AV planning/mapping benchmarks, and no cross-dataset or cross-city generalization experiments are shown.
The Association P-R metric is presented as a two-part incremental modification of existing Reachability P-R, limiting its methodological novelty despite being framed as a core contribution.

The manuscript contains numerous grammatical and typographical issues (e.g., repeated misspelling of "beam search" as "beem search," awkward phrasing throughout), suggesting insufficient polish for a top-tier venue submission.

Ablation results show spatial attention alone performs considerably worse than path-aware attention alone (62.1% vs 74.1% A-P50:95), and the marginal gain from combining them (+3.7%) is relatively modest, raising questions about how much the spatial attention component genuinely contributes beyond the topological attention.

No statistical significance testing, variance over multiple seeds/runs, or confidence intervals are reported for the main results or ablations, making it difficult to assess whether reported improvements are robust.

strengths: Addresses a practically important but understudied problem: associating online-constructed local HD maps with global SD maps for hybrid navigation, which is well-motivated with clear real-world relevance for autonomous driving stacks.

Introduces a new dataset (OMA/OMA-GT) built from nuScenes + OpenStreetMap with a reasonably large number of annotated road-lane correspondences, along with both ground-truth-HD and predicted-HD (MapTRv2) variants to test robustness to perception noise.
Proposes a tailored evaluation metric (Association P-R) that accounts for path-length bias and topological alignment, going beyond naive point-matching metrics like Reachability P-R.

The proposed Map Association Transformer (MAT) is a reasonably well-motivated architecture combining path-aware and spatial attention, and the paper provides fairly extensive ablations (structure, RoPE, loss terms, pooling, patch size, grouping strategy) as well as a model family (T/S/M/L) illustrating accuracy-latency trade-offs.
Supplementary material includes attention-map visualizations, qualitative comparisons, and failure-case analysis that add some interpretability to the claimed benefits of the dual-attention design.
weaknesses: Baselines are weak for a top-tier ML venue: only classical, non-learned methods (KNN, HMM) are compared against; despite the related-work section alluding to a 'contrastive learning framework' and other learned map-association ideas, no learned/deep-learning baseline other than the authors' own MAT family is evaluated, making it hard to assess whether the gains come from genuine architectural insight versus simply being the only learned method in the comparison.

The dataset's automated annotation pipeline relies on a MAT model pretrained on proprietary, non-releasable Chinese HD-SD map data to bootstrap nuScenes labels; this creates a reproducibility gap (the labeling pipeline itself cannot be fully reproduced or audited by outside researchers) and a potential circularity concern, since the benchmark's pseudo-ground-truth is partly generated by the same architecture proposed as the baseline method.

The paper explicitly acknowledges that MapTRv2-based HD map predictions used to build OMA are of questionable quality (4x oversegmented lanes, inflated lane-path counts, domain shift between train/val splits), and recommends future work not rely on MapTRv2 — this undermines confidence in the OMA (non-GT) benchmark numbers reported as core results.

The metric definition in the appendix (A-P50:95 as an unweighted sum over 10 thresholds, eq. 8) appears inconsistent with the main text's claim of following mAP convention (which averages, not sums) and does not match the actual reported table values (which remain under 100); this suggests either a typo or unclear/ambiguous metric specification that affects reproducibility.

Ablation studies are conducted only on OMA-GT (clean, ground-truth HD maps), not on the noisier OMA setting that is arguably more representative of real deployment, limiting insight into which architectural components matter most under realistic sensor/perception noise.

No code or dataset link is actually provided in the reviewed manuscript (placeholder left empty), and no discussion of licensing/availability details for the proprietary pretraining data used in annotation, raising practical reproducibility concerns.

The 'first benchmark/dataset' framing is not sufficiently differentiated from closely related SD-HD integration literature (e.g., the cited local-map-construction-with-SD-map survey), and the related work section is quite brief, limiting the reader's ability to judge true novelty versus incremental combination of existing ideas (MapTRv2, PTv3-style serialization, RoPE, CTC loss).

No statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or confidence intervals are reported for the main comparisons, and latency comparisons between GPU (MAT) and CPU (KNN/HMM, explicitly unoptimized Python/Numpy) are not entirely fair/apples-to-apples.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and practically relevant new task (Online Navigation Refinement / map association) bridging SD maps and online perception maps, addressing a real gap not covered by prior map matching or map generation literature.

Contributes a substantial new dataset (OMA) with 30K scenarios and 2.6M annotated lane vectors, built on nuScenes+OSM, with reasonable annotation quality checks (refinement ratio <1%) and clear train/val/test protocol including a distinct noisy test split using MapTRv2-generated OP maps.

Proposes a sensible, efficient architecture (MAT) with path-aware and spatial attention modules that have linear complexity, and demonstrates a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off (34-70ms) versus map-matching, graph-matching, and point-matching baselines.

Extensive ablations (patch size, grouping strategy, loss weighting, spatial curves, beam width, length intervals, distance thresholds, complexity-stratified metric, cross-city generalization, data efficiency, robustness to imperfect SD maps and environmental corruption) show reasonably thorough empirical validation and robustness analysis.

Proposes NR P-R, a new evaluation metric tailored to map-to-map association that separates geometric matching from semantic/topological correctness, which is a nontrivial and reasoned methodological contribution.
Reasonably strong reproducibility and ethics statements, with commitment to release code, data, and checkpoints, plus a detailed datasheet-style Q&A.
weaknesses: Baselines used for comparison (traditional map matching like HMM/DeepMM, graph matching KNN/GMT, point matching FastMAC) are not natively designed for the map-to-map lane-to-road association task and appear to be adapted/repurposed rather than strong tailored competitors; the comparison to more recent/relevant lane-topology or SD-prior-based perception methods (e.g., SMERF, P-MapNet, TopoSD, cited in related work) is absent, weakening the claim of state-of-the-art performance for this specific task.

The overall absolute performance on the (more realistic) noisy Test set is quite low (NR-F1 ~41-55%), raising concerns about real-world readiness/maturity of the proposed pipeline despite latency and relative-improvement claims.

Reliance on a single source dataset (nuScenes, only Boston and Singapore) for both training and evaluation limits geographic and sensor/perception-model diversity; cross-validation between only two cities is a fairly weak test of generalization given both are urban coastal cities within the same dataset collection protocol.

The dependency of the Test set OP maps on a single perception model (MapTRv2) for the main experiments (with only a small supplementary test in appendix using MapTR/SeqGrowGraph) could bias results toward errors specific to this model's failure modes.

Some claims (e.g., 'first' benchmark, 'best performance') are strongly asserted without deeper discussion of limitations such as annotation ambiguity at lane transitions (acknowledged only briefly in appendix) or potential subjectivity in manual road-lane association labeling.

The paper is dense with many contributions (dataset, metric, model) that dilutes the depth of methodological novelty for each; the core attention mechanisms (path-aware ordering + spatial curve serialization) are relatively incremental combinations of existing techniques (group attention, Hilbert curve serialization, topological ordering) rather than fundamentally new ideas.

Latency claims are reported only on a single high-end GPU/CPU combination (A6000 + Xeon 8369B) without discussion of edge/mobile deployment feasibility, which is relevant given the paper's motivation of 'low-cost' navigation.

strengths: Addresses a practically motivated and under-explored problem: aligning SD maps with online perception (OP) maps to obtain lane-level navigation without relying on costly HD maps.
Contributes a large-scale annotated dataset (OMA) with manual lane-to-road correspondence annotations, which did not previously exist publicly for this exact setting.

Provides an extensive set of ablations and robustness studies (cross-city generalization, data efficiency, noise injection on SD maps, environmental corruption via nuScenes-C, different OP map generators), showing effort toward thorough empirical validation.
The proposed NR P-R metric with length-interval stratification and distance-threshold matching is reasonably well-motivated and detailed with pseudocode.
Achieves low inference latency (34 ms), which is relevant for the claimed real-time application scenario.
Good qualitative visualizations (attention maps, comparison figures, failure case analysis) that aid interpretability.
weaknesses: The chosen baselines (HMM, DeepMM, MTrajRec, GraphMM, EAM3, KNN, GMT, FastMAC) were not designed for the map-to-map association setting; adapting path-to-map matching or generic graph/point matching methods to this new task without task-specific tuning risks producing weak strawman comparisons that inflate the apparent improvement of MAT.

Absolute performance on the test set remains low (NR-F1 ranging ~42-55% depending on the OP generator), and the complexity-weighted analysis in the appendix shows severe degradation on curved/complex roads (down to ~10-12% on the test set for high-complexity bins), undermining the claim that the method provides a practically reliable solution for real-world lane-level navigation.

There is a large and somewhat artificial distributional gap between train/val (using ground-truth OP maps) and test (using MapTRv2-generated OP maps), with test-set statistics showing roughly 4x more lanes/scene and much higher fragmentation than train/val — this raises questions about whether the test set evaluation is representative or overly adversarial/skewed.

The core technical novelty is incremental: path-aware attention and spatial attention are essentially reordering-plus-grouped-attention schemes closely related to existing serialization-based transformers (e.g., Point Transformer V3, explicitly used as the ablation baseline), applied to a new domain rather than introducing fundamentally new architectural ideas.

The method depends on hand-engineered topological-constraint beam search post-processing to fix predicted topology errors, suggesting the learned association head alone does not robustly capture topological consistency.

Dataset diversity is limited to two cities from nuScenes (Boston, Singapore); the cross-validation claims of 'good geographical generalizability' are weakly supported by such a narrow city pool, and broader domain generalization (e.g., different countries/road conventions) remains unverified.

Reliance on manual annotation for lane-to-road correspondences raises scalability concerns for extending the benchmark; the proposed 'human-in-the-loop' future expansion strategy is speculative and not empirically validated in this paper.
Writing quality has minor issues (grammatical inconsistencies in the abstract and elsewhere), suggesting the manuscript could benefit from more careful proofreading.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and practically relevant new task (Online Navigation Refinement) that addresses a real gap between cheap, globally-consistent SD maps and locally accurate but topology-lacking OP maps.

Contributes a sizeable, manually annotated benchmark dataset (OMA) with over 30K scenarios and 2.6M lane vectors, along with a documented, structured annotation workflow and data statement (motivation, distribution, maintenance, composition) in the appendix.

Proposes a lightweight transformer (MAT) with path-aware and spatial attention modules that are conceptually well-motivated (topological vs. geometric locality) and empirically shown to be complementary via ablations.
Strong real-time performance (34-70ms) while outperforming a wide range of baselines (traditional MM, seq2seq, graph matching, point matching) on both validation and multi-generator test sets.

Extensive supplementary experiments: cross-city validation (Boston/Singapore), data efficiency study showing strong low-data performance, robustness to imperfect/noisy SD maps, robustness to environmental corruptions (nuScenes-C) in a zero-shot setting, and generalization across different OP map generators (MapTR, MapTRv2, SeqGrowGraph).
Careful design of the NR P-R metric with length- and curvature-based stratification to avoid biasing evaluation toward short/simple paths, plus ablations justifying threshold and interval choices.
Reasonable reproducibility and ethics statements, with plans to release code, checkpoints, and annotations.
weaknesses: The dataset is derived entirely from nuScenes (only Boston and Singapore), limiting geographic and road-network diversity; claims of strong geographical generalization rest on a fairly narrow two-city cross-validation.

There is a large gap between validation (NR-F1 ~78-79%) and test set performance (NR-F1 ~42-55%), indicating that under realistic OP map noise the method's absolute performance is still fairly limited; this discrepancy could be discussed more critically as a limitation of real-world readiness.

Baseline comparisons (HMM, DeepMM, MTrajRec, GraphMM, EAM3, KNN, GMT, FastMAC) are largely adapted from path-to-map matching or generic graph/point matching, not originally designed for the many-to-one lane-to-road association setting; it is not entirely clear these baselines were tuned as carefully as MAT, raising some concern about comparison fairness.

The test set OP maps depend heavily on a single perception model (MapTRv2) for training-time evaluation choices, and though the authors test other generators, the core benchmark construction and threshold tuning are somewhat tied to this specific model's noise characteristics.

The curvature/complexity-stratified analysis in the appendix reveals that performance drops sharply on high-curvature or complex topology paths (e.g., 87.2% to 43.1% on Val across complexity bins), suggesting the main reported NR-F1 numbers may overstate performance on the harder, more navigation-critical scenarios (intersections, curves).

No real-vehicle or closed-loop navigation evaluation is provided; all validation is via offline map-association metrics, so the actual impact on lane-level navigation quality in practice remains unverified.

Some design choices (e.g., PTv3 as baseline backbone, exact beam search formulation) are only lightly justified in the main text and require appendix cross-referencing, slightly hurting self-containedness and clarity.
